note: Topic queue for the twice-weekly blog cadence. The publishing routine picks the first topic whose slug is not already in blog-posts.json, writes a full post from the brief, and ships it. Add more topics to the end of the list to extend the cadence; edit freely. Ordering is deliberate near the front: topics with measured search demand in Search Console sit ahead of evergreen ones, so the cadence spends its next slots where impressions already exist. Briefs that name a sector and a constraint (a small team, a utility, a district, a defense supplier) get cited by AI assistants far more than generic explainers, so prefer that framing. Provenance: the demand-ranked run at the front, sftp-vs-ftps-vs-tftp through hitech-vs-hipaa, was ordered on Google Search Console impressions for Aug 4 to 29, 2026, the property's first four weeks of data (file transfer 407, tcp 262, pdpa 225, scim 173, ptes 120, otp 105, dfars 83, nerc 76, ferpa 65, hitech/hipaa 63, chfi 49; iso-27001-annex-a-tour sits last on 32 impressions but holds the site's best average position, 46.6). Networking protocol acronyms were the largest cluster in that data and had no coverage at all, hence the three transport and file transfer additions. Bing Webmaster data was unavailable at the time, so this ranking is Google only. Re-measure before reshuffling this run rather than reordering it on intuition.

topics.title: NordVPN Review: What a VPN Actually Protects (and What It Never Will)
topics.brief: An honest practitioner review of NordVPN. Open with a clear one-sentence affiliate disclosure near the top that links to /disclosure/ (the post contains affiliate links and the site may earn a commission at no extra cost to the reader). Be direct that a VPN is not a silver bullet: it encrypts traffic in transit and hides your IP from the local network and your ISP, but it does not stop phishing, malware, credential theft, or a breached service leaking your data, and HTTPS already protects most sessions. Then cover where NordVPN genuinely earns a place in a layered setup: public Wi-Fi and travel, untrusted networks, IP privacy, and testing region-dependent behavior. Discuss NordLynx (WireGuard) performance, the independently audited no-logs policy, and why the bundled Threat Protection feature is a nice extra but no replacement for real endpoint protection. Briefly contrast consumer VPNs with corporate remote-access VPNs and with zero trust approaches like ZTNA and SASE so readers understand the category. Close with who should buy it (frequent travelers, public Wi-Fi users, privacy-conscious readers) and who can skip it. Every NordVPN call-to-action link in the post must use the tracking URL https://www.anrdoezrs.net/click-8024903-13756265 with plain-language anchor text.

topics.title: NordPass Review: A Password Manager Is Step One, Not the Whole Plan
topics.brief: An honest practitioner review of the NordPass password manager. Open with a clear one-sentence affiliate disclosure near the top that links to /disclosure/ (the post contains affiliate links and the site may earn a commission at no extra cost to the reader). Frame the problem first: password reuse is what makes credential stuffing work, and a password manager is the single highest-leverage habit fix for most people. Review NordPass on its merits: XChaCha20 encryption, zero-knowledge architecture, breach monitoring, passkey support, email masking, and cross-device sync. Be honest about limits: a password manager does not stop phishing on its own (users can still be tricked into filling credentials on look-alike sites), the master password is a single point of failure that itself needs strong MFA, browser autofill has known edge cases, and unique passwords do nothing if a service is breached and MFA is absent. Position it inside a layered identity stack: pair it with MFA everywhere, prefer phishing-resistant methods like FIDO2 passkeys over SMS or TOTP where offered, and note that enterprise credential problems need SSO and PAM, not a consumer vault. Close with who benefits most (anyone reusing passwords today) and a realistic setup path. Every NordPass call-to-action link must use the tracking URL https://www.anrdoezrs.net/click-8024903-15112066 with plain-language anchor text.

topics.title: Sucuri Review: A WAF for Your Website, Not a Substitute for Patching
topics.brief: An honest practitioner review of the Sucuri website security platform for small-site owners (WordPress and other CMS-run sites). Open with a clear one-sentence affiliate disclosure near the top that links to /disclosure/ (the post contains affiliate links and the site may earn a commission at no extra cost to the reader). Explain what the product actually is: a cloud WAF and CDN that sits in front of the site filtering XSS, SQL injection, and bot traffic, plus DDoS mitigation, malware scanning, and a cleanup/incident-response service if a site is already hacked. Highlight real strengths: virtual patching buys time when a CVE drops for a plugin you cannot update immediately, the cleanup service has a strong reputation, and flat pricing is simple. Be honest about limits: a WAF is a filter, not a fix; it cannot patch the CMS or plugins for you, rules can be bypassed, and if the origin server IP leaks (DNS history, misconfiguration) attackers can go around the WAF entirely, so origin lockdown matters. Scanning is detection, not prevention, and remote scanners can miss server-side malware. The boring fundamentals still carry the weight: timely updates, least-privilege admin accounts, MFA on the CMS login, and tested backups. Close with who it fits (site owners without a security team, anyone mid-incident needing cleanup) and who should rely on fundamentals first. Every Sucuri call-to-action link must use the tracking URL https://www.anrdoezrs.net/click-8024903-13942196 with plain-language anchor text.

topics.title: How to Remove Yourself From Data Broker Sites (Free and Paid Ways)
topics.brief: A practical guide to getting your personal information off data broker and people-search sites. Open with a clear one-sentence affiliate disclosure near the top that links to /disclosure/ (the post contains an affiliate link and the site may earn a commission at no extra cost to the reader). Explain the problem first: brokers scrape public records and resold data into profiles (home address, phone, relatives, income) that fuel phishing, doxxing, stalking, and identity theft, and this data is prime OSINT for attackers. Cover the free DIY route honestly and thoroughly: CCPA and CPRA give California residents a legal right to opt out, most major brokers honor requests nationwide, and readers can work through the biggest offenders (Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified, Radaris) by hand; be honest that DIY is a treadmill because profiles repopulate and there are 600+ brokers, so budget for repeating the exercise quarterly. Then cover paid automation: Optery is the option this site partners with (mention its free exposure report as a no-cost first step, and PCMag's repeated Editors' Choice awards); every Optery call-to-action link must use the tracking URL https://get.optery.com/rhg204bv4giz with plain-language anchor text. Name DeleteMe and Incogni as credible alternatives worth comparing (plain unmonetized mentions, which is consistent with this site's editorial independence). Close with the honest boundary: removal services shrink your public footprint but cannot recall breached or sold data, so pair this with unique passwords and MFA. Cross-link the PII, OSINT, CCPA, and BEC glossary pages inline.
